questions.question: Doxycycline mechanism of action, interactions, treatment durations, and use as STI post-exposure prophylaxis.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action of doxycycline?
What substance or medication, when taken with doxycycline, reduces its efficacy, and why?
Complete this table regarding duration of doxycycline for community-acquired pneumonia, chlamydial urethritis, and lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV).
How would you counsel someone to take doxycycline as post-exposure prophylaxis for prevention of a sexually transmitted infection?

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism of action of Doxycycline?
What substance or medication that when taken with Doxycycline reduces its efficacy AND why?
Complete this table regarding duration of doxycycline for: Community Acquired Pneumonia; Chlamydia urethritis; LGV
How would you counsel someone to take Doxycycline as post-exposure prophylaxis for prevention of STI?

questions.model_answer:
a) Doxycycline inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by reversibly binding the 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosomal acceptor (A) site, thereby preventing peptide-chain elongation; because binding is reversible it is bacteriostatic.
b) Multivalent (divalent/trivalent) cations — aluminum, calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc — found in antacids, dairy/milk, sucralfate, didanosine, and multivitamins. They chelate doxycycline in the gut, reducing its absorption (by up to 50–90% for the class), which lowers serum levels and efficacy; separate ingestion by at least 2–3 hours.
c) (1) Community-acquired pneumonia: ~5–7 days (not specified in this chapter; IDSA/ATS minimum 5 days). (2) Chlamydial (non-gonococcal) urethritis: 100 mg PO BID x 7 days. (3) LGV: 100 mg PO BID x 21 days.
d) Doxy-PEP: take a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline by mouth, as soon as possible and ideally within 24 hours (no later than 72 hours) after condomless oral, vaginal, or anal sex; do not exceed 200 mg per 24-hour period; take with a full glass of water while upright to avoid pill esophagitis; it reduces chlamydia, syphilis, and (less so) gonorrhea but does not replace condoms or HIV prevention.
questions.beyond_mandell: CAP duration and the formal doxy-PEP regimen (single 200 mg within 72 h of condomless sex) are from IDSA/ATS CAP guidance and the CDC 2024 doxy-PEP guideline, not this chapter; the chapter only references a pilot trial of daily prophylactic doxycycline.

questions.question: Tigecycline susceptibility and mechanism of action.

parts.text: Are the following bacteria generally susceptible to tigecycline, and if not, what is the mechanism of resistance? Pseudomonas; Acinetobacter; Morganella; vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE).
What is tigecycline's mechanism of action?

parts_raw.text: Are the following bacteria generally susceptible to Tigecycline and if no, what is the mechanism of resistance? Pseudomonas; Acinetobacter; Morganella; VRE

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Pseudomonas aeruginosa — No; intrinsically resistant due to the MexXY multidrug efflux pump. (2) Acinetobacter spp. — Yes; tigecycline remains one of the most active agents against Acinetobacter. (3) Morganella morganii — No; intrinsic resistance from drug recognition/upregulation by the AcrAB (and MexAB-OprM) multidrug efflux pumps. (4) VRE — Yes; active against enterococci, including VanA, VanB, and VanC vancomycin-resistant phenotypes.
b) Tigecycline is a glycylcycline (semisynthetic minocycline derivative). Like other tetracyclines it inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking entry of aminoacyl-tRNA into the A site and preventing incorporation of amino acids into the elongating peptide chain; it is bacteriostatic (reversible binding). Its 9-glycyl substituent binds the ribosome ~5-fold more strongly, letting it overcome efflux- and ribosomal-protection (tet) resistance.

cohort_answer.text: Pseudomonas - no, multidrug efflux pump. Acinetobacter - yes. Morganella - no, multidrug efflux pump (AcrAB). VRE - yes (only Vanco susceptible E. faecalis). MOA: glycylcycline; binds bacterial 30S ribosome, blocks tRNA entry, prevents protein synthesis limiting bacterial growth.

questions.question: Tigecycline compared with piperacillin-tazobactam.

parts.text: Two advantages of tigecycline over piperacillin-tazobactam.
Two organisms not covered by tigecycline.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Broader coverage of resistant (antibiotic-resistant) organisms that piperacillin-tazobactam does not reliably cover — MRSA, VRE, and ESBL-/AmpC-/carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, plus Acinetobacter and atypicals. (2) Favourable pharmacokinetics — no dose adjustment needed in renal impairment and not significantly removed by hemodialysis, with simple fixed BID dosing.
b) (1) Pseudomonas aeruginosa (intrinsically resistant). (2) Proteus spp. (also Providencia and Morganella) — both are covered by piperacillin-tazobactam.

cohort_answer.text: a) PK: less frequent (BID) dosing, no renal/HD adjustment needed. PD: coverage of AROs incl MRSA, VRE, ESBL, AmpCs, CRE, atypicals, NTM, Nocardia. b) Pseudomonas; Proteus mirabilis; Providencia; Morganella.

questions.model_answer:
Tigecycline / Ertapenem / Colistin:
Acinetobacter: S / R / S
Stenotrophomonas: S / R / S
Pseudomonas: R / R / S
Proteus: R / S / R
ESBL: S / S / S
(Key points: Pseudomonas is intrinsically resistant to both tigecycline and ertapenem but susceptible to colistin; Proteus is intrinsically resistant to both tigecycline and colistin; ESBL Enterobacterales remain susceptible to all three.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Intrinsic-resistance grid is not tabulated in the pp. 407-409 slice; answered from established intrinsic-resistance patterns (the slice does note colistin-resistant Serratia and Stenotrophomonas superinfection, p. 409).

cohort_answer.text: Acinetobacter: S/R/S. Steno: S/R/S. Pseudomonas: R/R/S. Proteus: R/S/R. ESBL: S/S/S.

questions.model_answer: a) Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem (carbapenems lower antiepileptic levels). b) Atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency). c) Doxycycline over Septra/TMP-SMX (not used to treat CDI and low risk of inducing CDI). d) Fluconazole over caspofungin (superior renal/urinary penetration; echinocandins negligible in urine). e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir (superior anti-CMV activity). f) Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (for bacteria in the CNS).
questions.beyond_mandell: Antibacterial/antifungal pairings draw on general ID pharmacology; only the CMV/herpesvirus activity claim (valganciclovir) is grounded in Mandell Ch. 46.

cohort_answer.text: a) Pip/Tazo over Mero because patient on tegretol. b) Atovaquone over Dapsone because patient has G6PD deficiency. c) Doxycycline over Septra because drug not used for CDI treatment and not associated with development of CDI. d) Fluconazole over Caspofungin because it has superior renal penetration. e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir because it works better for CMV. f) Moxifloxacin over Levofloxacin because it works better for a bacteria in the CNS.

questions.question: Name three antibiotics with gram-negative coverage to which Proteus and Providencia are intrinsically resistant.

parts.text: Name three antibiotics with gram-negative coverage that are intrinsically resistant to Proteus and Providencia.

parts_raw.text: Name three antibiotics with gram negative coverage that are intrinsically resistant to proteus and providencia

questions.model_answer: (1) Nitrofurantoin (2) Polymyxins (colistin/polymyxin B) (3) Tigecycline. (Proteus spp. and Providencia spp. are intrinsically resistant to all three despite their general gram-negative activity.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Intrinsic-resistance patterns per EUCAST Expert Rules / CLSI; the chapter notes Proteus resists methenamine via urease-driven alkaline urine but does not tabulate this list.
